# Restoration Modes {#sec-modes}

A project does not turn out restorative. Somebody decides which lever will carry that work and commits the design to it, early enough that the decision survives the last round of cost cutting. That choice is the project's [**restoration mode**](terminology.qmd#term-restoration-mode), and it is the third thing this document puts on a project. [Scale](scale-transect.qmd) says what was available. The [siting axis](siting-axis.qmd) says what happened to production. The mode says which lever actually did the restoring, which is the one of the three a designer chooses outright.

## The five modes {#sec-lv-mode}

Five of the six [design levers](design-levers.qmd) can be made to carry the work.

- **[Siting-led](terminology.qmd#term-siting-led)** — put the array where the ground itself does the work. [Solar prairie strips](archetypes.qmd#arch-prairie-strips) are the case: the planting goes where the runoff already goes.
- **[Structure-led](terminology.qmd#term-structure-led)** — build the geometry to do it: clearance, row spacing, how much light the modules let through. [Barnyard shelter](archetypes.qmd#arch-barnyard) is the case.
- **[Management-led](terminology.qmd#term-management-led)** — take placement as given and put the ground cover, the grazing regime, and the operational calendar to work. Regenerative solar grazing is the case.
- **[Ownership-led](terminology.qmd#term-ownership-led)** — structure the holding so that no agreement is required, because the interests were never opposed. [Barnyard shelter](archetypes.qmd#arch-barnyard) is the case again, and for a second reason: the person who owns the array owns the animals standing under it.
- **[Contract-led](terminology.qmd#term-contract-led)** — write it into the lease, the ordinance, or the benefit agreement rather than into anything on the site. The [community and economic function](restorative-functions.qmd#sec-fn-community) runs on this one.

**Ownership-led and contract-led are the same problem at two scales.** An owner-operator needs nothing written down, because the party deciding and the party living with the decision are one person. A utility in another state needs everything written down, because they are not. So the alignment that ownership supplies for free at the farmstead has to be manufactured, clause by clause, as ownership moves up the transect: the lease term, the maintenance obligation, the benefit agreement, the decommissioning bond. **Contract-led restoration is what you need when ownership-led restoration is no longer available**, which is why it is nearly empty at the farmstead and the main instrument at utility scale, exactly where ownership has travelled furthest from the ground.

## Scale decides which modes stay open {#sec-restoration-modes}

**Scale is not itself a restoration mode. It governs all the others.** Choosing to build five megawatts rather than eighty is not a way of doing restorative work; it is what decides which of the five stay open to the design. That is the argument the [scale transect](scale-transect.qmd) makes at length, and why that chapter can say which mode dominates at each zone (§-@sec-restoration-modes).

That may not hold. Solar's spillover benefits scale with perimeter and proximity rather than with area, which makes several mid-sized arrays a different ecological proposition from one large one at the same capacity (§-@sec-community-scale). If that argument survives measurement, choosing to build small and many *is* restorative work, and scale earns a mode after all. Nobody has run the comparison (§-@sec-open-issues).

Leverage is about what is available. The [restoration mode](terminology.qmd#term-restoration-mode) is which lever a design puts to work, and because the levers trade against each other the mode a project can realistically choose changes along the transect. At A1 the operator controls the hardware and has almost no ground to choose among, so the work is **[structure-led](terminology.qmd#term-structure-led)**. Through A2 and A3 latitude opens and placement becomes the strongest instrument available, so it is **[siting-led](terminology.qmd#term-siting-led)**. By A4 and A5 the ground has been chosen by other forces entirely, and restoration is carried by what grows and how it is run, so it is **[management-led](terminology.qmd#term-management-led)**. At utility scale restorative practice is mainly ground cover and grazing; at small and mid scale it is mainly placement [@macknick2022; @boggis2020].

Those other forces can be named. Across US [utility-scale](terminology.qmd#term-utility-scale) projects, siting tracks proximity to roads, transmission lines, and substations, together with higher population density, non-forested cover, and flatter terrain [@wu2026siting]. None of those is a property of the ground that restoration cares about. A parcel is selected because a substation is close and the slope is mild, and whether it was leaching nitrate or carrying a wet depression enters the decision late or not at all. That is the mechanism behind the phrase *assembly-driven*, and it is why siting-led restoration is a middle-of-the-transect instrument rather than a large-project one.

The economics point the same way, and harder. Greenfield sites, prime agricultural land above all, deliver the lowest levelized cost of any land class, roughly \$39 to \$57 per MWh, while contaminated land carries a cost premium of 14 to 33% and limited technical potential besides [@owusuobeng2025]. So the ground that a restorative argument most wants taken is the ground a cost model most wants avoided, and the gap widens with project size because a developer assembling several hundred contiguous acres has fewer candidate parcels and less appetite for a premium on any of them. [Brightfields](archetypes.qmd#arch-brightfield) exist, and they do not scale for this reason rather than for a technical one.

::: {.caution}
**What these two sources do and do not show.** @wu2026siting is a study of utility-scale projects, at a 1 MW floor, and it treats each project as a single observation. It does not test whether siting drivers differ by project size, so it establishes what large-project siting responds to without establishing the contrast this section draws against smaller projects. That contrast still rests on @macknick2022 and @boggis2020 and on the archetypes, which is weaker evidence than a size-stratified analysis would be, and is why the peak of siting latitude remains an open question (§-@sec-oi-vocabulary, issue 2). @owusuobeng2025 is a preprint and has not been through review.
:::

## Choosing the mode, and checking it {#sec-mode-choose}

Choosing the mode early keeps a design from spending itself on a lever that scale has already closed. At A4 there is little to be gained by arguing over ground the interconnection queue has effectively chosen, and a great deal to be gained by writing the seed mix and the maintenance obligation into the lease. Naming the mode is how that gets decided on purpose rather than by default, and defaulting is how a project ends up with restorative intentions and gravel.

Grazing shows the whole set working at once. It is a management decision that only pays if the structure left clearance for the animals, the contract found somebody to keep them, and the scale is large enough to be worth a grazier's drive, which is why grazing arrangements fall apart for reasons that have nothing to do with grazing.

Naming the mode also settles two things after the fact. What to copy: a design that worked because of where it sat will not transfer to a site without that ground, however carefully the rest is reproduced, which is the mechanism behind [design import](terminology.qmd#term-design-import) (§-@sec-rg-consequences). And what to check: a siting-led claim is verified against a map, a structure-led claim against a drawing, a management-led claim against a maintenance schedule somebody has to keep for thirty years, and a contract-led claim against a document that can be read.
